Updates `wrangler` from 4.160.0 to 4.164.0
Release notes

Sourced from wrangler's releases.

wrangler@4.164.0

Minor Changes

  • #16450 5f05841 Thanks @​xortive! - Add custom CA and client certificate references to Workers VPC service TLS settings

    Workers VPC (open beta) service create and update commands accept --certificate-authority and --client-certificate UUIDs. Use either flag alone or both together. Whenever you supply either reference, explicitly choose --cert-verification-mode:

    • verify_full: verify the origin certificate chain and hostname (the platform default).
    • verify_ca: verify the chain but skip hostname verification, weakening origin identity checks.
    • disabled: do not verify the origin certificate; this allows connections to impersonated origins and is unsafe for production.

    For HTTP services, these settings apply to HTTPS connections, not plaintext HTTP. TCP services can use them for upstream TLS, including PostgreSQL.

    TLS settings are per-service only: host and resolver networks have no TLS settings or inheritance. Omitting TLS settings uses platform defaults (certificate chain and hostname verification). Explicit mode-only configuration, including verify_full, is accepted. A custom CA cannot be combined with disabled; a client certificate without a custom CA can.

    Upload certificates using the existing commands, then use the returned IDs below. Replace <ca-uuid>, <client-uuid>, <tunnel-uuid>, and service IDs with your own values; certificate references must be valid UUIDs. Upload replacement certificates the same way before rotating their references.

    pnpm exec wrangler cert upload certificate-authority --ca-cert ./ca.pem --name private-ca
pnpm exec wrangler cert upload mtls-certificate --cert ./client.pem --key ./client-key.pem --name private-client

    Create an HTTPS service with both a custom trust chain and an mTLS client certificate, or a PostgreSQL TCP service with only a custom CA:

    pnpm exec wrangler vpc service create private-web \
  --type http --https-port 443 --ipv4 10.0.0.10 --tunnel-id <tunnel-uuid> \
  --certificate-authority <ca-uuid> --client-certificate <client-uuid> \
  --cert-verification-mode verify_full

    pnpm exec wrangler vpc service create private-db 
    
--type tcp --tcp-port 5432 --app-protocol postgresql 
    
--hostname db.internal.example --resolver-ips 10.0.0.53 --tunnel-id <tunnel-uuid> 
    
--certificate-authority <ca-uuid> --cert-verification-mode verify_full

    For client-certificate-only configuration, use --client-certificate <client-uuid> --cert-verification-mode verify_full instead of the certificate flags in either create command.

    Updates replace the complete service configuration, including TLS settings, in a single request, the same as cf workers-vpc services update. Pass every TLS option the service should keep: certificate references and the verification mode that you omit are cleared, and an update without TLS options returns the service to the platform defaults. Removing a reference releases its backend certificate binding but does not delete the uploaded account certificate. For example, rotate the web service's client certificate while keeping its CA:

    pnpm exec wrangler vpc service update <web-service-uuid> \
  --name private-web --type http --https-port 443 \
  --ipv4 10.0.0.10 --tunnel-id <tunnel-uuid> \
  --certificate-authority <ca-uuid> --client-certificate <replacement-client-uuid> \
  --cert-verification-mode verify_full

    To remove the CA while keeping the client certificate, repeat the update with only --client-certificate <client-uuid> and a verification mode.

... (truncated)

Updates `pixi.js` from 8.22.0 to 8.23.0
Release notes

Sourced from pixi.js's releases.

v8.23.0

💾 Download

Installation:

npm install pixi.js@8.23.0

Development Build:

  • https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pixi.js@8.23.0/dist/pixi.js

Documentation:

  • https://pixijs.download/v8.23.0/docs/index.html

Changed

https://github.com/pixijs/pixijs/compare/v8.22.0...v8.23.0

🚨 Behavior Change

  • fix: deliver global move events to interactive ancestors once and trim per-target dispatch work by @​GoodBoyDigital in pixijs/pixijs#12329
    • An interactive ancestor of the object under the pointer, such as an interactive app.stage, now receives globalpointermove, globalmousemove and globaltouchmove once per move instead of twice. This applies to listeners and to on* handler properties. Code that counted these calls or added up movement per call will see half as many calls.
  • chore: merge the PixiJS agent skills into one pixijs skill by @​Zyie in pixijs/pixijs#12384
    • PixiJS now ships one pixijs agent skill in node_modules/pixi.js/skills/ in place of the separate pixijs-* skills. Point any agent setup that loads or names an old skill, such as pixijs-scene-sprite, at skills/pixijs instead.

🎁 Added

  • feat: add SmoothGraphics with shader-based HHAA anti-aliasing by @​Zyie in pixijs/pixijs#12002
    • New SmoothGraphics is a Graphics that anti-aliases its edges in the shader, so shapes and thin lines stay smooth without MSAA, at any scale and inside render textures. It has the same drawing API as Graphics, and a DashLineShader set as its context's customShader draws the strokes dashed and hides the fills, with dash and gap changeable without rebuilding geometry. A GraphicsContext drawn by both a Graphics and a SmoothGraphics can render blank in one of them without an error, so give one of them a context.clone().
    import { DashLineShader, SmoothGraphics } from 'pixi.js';

    const smooth = new SmoothGraphics()
    
.circle(100, 100, 50)
    
.fill(0xde3249)
    
.stroke({ width: 1, color: 0xffffff });
    

    const dashed = new SmoothGraphics();
    

    dashed.context.customShader = new DashLineShader({ dash: 10, gap: 5 });
    
dashed.moveTo(0, 0).lineTo(200, 0).stroke({ width: 2, color: 0xffffff });
    

    app.stage.addChild(smooth, dashed);

  • feat: add safariFontDelay option for HTMLText by @​vtxe02023274 in pixijs/pixijs#12324
    • The new safariFontDelay renderer option sets how many milliseconds HTMLText waits before drawing in Safari, where embedded fonts may not be ready yet. It defaults to 100, the previous fixed delay. Set it to 0 to skip the wait when your fonts are already loaded in the document, at init or later through renderer.htmlText.safariFontDelay.

Updates `preact-render-to-string` from 6.8.2 to 6.8.3
Release notes

Sourced from preact-render-to-string's releases.

v6.8.3

Patch Changes

  • #494 b217ca7 Thanks @​JoviDeCroock! - Handle streaming errors the way React does. An error below a Suspense boundary is reported through onError and the boundary is left to the client, only an error outside of every boundary fails the render (onShellError). Aborting reports every pending boundary, hands it to the client and ends the response, as does a destination that closes early or a cancelled renderToReadableStream.

  • #480 c44af38 Thanks @​JoviDeCroock! - Render Suspense fallbacks for recoverable values during string and streaming renders.

  • #491 15daddd Thanks @​JoviDeCroock! - Skip on* props instead of serializing them as attributes, matching Preact, which only binds function values as event listeners.

  • #493 aa58c1c Thanks @​saxymofo! - Set the component's _globalContext so use(Context) from preact/compat (Preact 11) resolves the nearest provider instead of throwing.

Updates `ws` from 8.22.1 to 8.23.0
Release notes

Sourced from ws's releases.

8.23.0

Features

  • Introduced the maxPendingAutoPongs option (ace7248f).

Bug fixes

  • Fixed a remote memory exhaustion DoS vulnerability (ace7248f).

A malicious peer can flood the other peer with Ping frames while stopping reads, forcing it to buffer Pong frames that are automatically sent in response until memory is exhausted, leading to process termination due to OOM.

import { WebSocket, WebSocketServer } from 'ws';

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 0 }, function () {
const data = Buffer.alloc(125);
const { port } = wss.address();
const ws = new WebSocket(ws://localhost:${port});


ws.on('open', function () {
ws.pause();


(function ping() {
  ws.ping(data, function (err) {
    if (err) return;
    ping();
  });
})();



});


ws.on('error', console.error);
ws.on('close', function (code, reason) {
console.log(client close - code: ${code} reason: ${reason.toString()});
});
});


wss.on('connection', function (ws) {
ws.on('error', console.error);
ws.on('close', function (code, reason) {
console.log(server close - code: ${code} reason: ${reason.toString()});
});
});

The vulnerability was responsibly disclosed by multiple reporters:

  • G0r4ni8

Added

  • vtc: A VTC can take a level-1 did:webs as its own DID (#2698)

  • feat(vta-sdk): vtc-host-classical, the VTC template a level-1 did:webs can carry

    A level-1 did:webs holds one key-state signing key, and CONVENTIONS.md 0.2 §9.2 refuses vtc-host's second (post-quantum) signing slot as keyAlgorithm and forbids a VTA to drop what a template describes; the template keys block has no optional slot (vta/did-templates/* 3.1). So a did:webs VTC (VTI-KEY-001) names a template that does not ask for the key: vtc-host-classical, vtc-host less the pq-signing slot, its verification method and its assertionMethod reference. It is derived from vtc-host when loaded, not shipped as a second file, so the two cannot drift (pinned by a test rendering both). The §9.2 check is unchanged: vtc-host stays refused, every other refusal stands.

    The §9.2 service rule reads a {DID}#… id as the DID's own fragment: a service supplied whole as a variable (SERVICE_TSP, SERVICE_DIDCOMM) keeps the placeholder, because a whole-value substitution is not substituted again, and was refused under did:webs as "not a fragment".

  • vta: Provision an integration as a did:webs (#2695)

The template var DID_METHOD=webs routes provision-integration's mint to create_did_webs: level 1, class service (VTI-KEY-192), shaped by the template with every CONVENTIONS.md 0.2 §9.2 check and refusal, gated by [dids] webs_service_dids, and published at WEBVH_SERVER (required: a did:webs has no serverless mode) on WEBVH_DOMAIN under WEBVH_PATH. No wire member is added to provision/integration/0.3: the method is a template var, as DID_METHOD=scid already was. A build without webs refuses the selection by name.

The bundle stays SealedPayloadV1::TemplateBootstrap. Its keys are the key-state key and the designated X25519 key agreement key under the ids the did:webs document gives them (#), config.did_document is the document the stream derives, and the stream itself rides a new TemplateOutput::WebsKeriCesr in place of a did.jsonl. It is emitted only for a did:webs, so every webvh/did:key/did:peer bundle is byte-identical; an opener that predates the variant refuses such a bundle by name. Banyan

Coordinated OpenVTC release Banyan — a known-good, cross-project snapshot of all OpenVTC projects. Tagged at the main-branch HEAD on 2026-06-23.

Changelog

Sourced from dtg-credentials's changelog.

[0.14.0] - 2026-11-10

Breaking: a VAC states purposes of use (DTG Core Credentials, context v2), and verify_chain holds a chain to them — see Changed (breaking) below.

Added

  • A VAC states purposes of use (DTG Core Credentials, Purposes of Use; trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#84). credentialSubject.purposes is optional, {"scope":"any"} or {"scope":"listed","purposes":[...]} with a non-empty list of registered names or absolute IRIs, each once; absent means any, and any never grants modelTraining. dtg_credentials::purposes::PurposeScope models it, read strictly (an any carrying purposes, an empty list or a duplicate is refused at parse). A VAC stating it lists DTG_CONTEXT_V2 (https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/context/v2) second, which is now recognized beside v1; a VAC stating it under v1 is refused.
  • verify_chain enforces the chain rule and reports the effective purposes. A link stating none takes its parent's; a link stating purposes its parent does not grant is AuthorityError::WidensPurposes. The root states the grant, so only a root naming modelTraining can pass it on. VerifiedAuthority::purposes carries the result.
  • DTGCredential::with_purposes states them (switching the context to v2), and with_purposes_under refuses at issue purposes wider than those the parent states.

Changed (breaking)

  • CredentialSubjectAuthority gains purposes, VerifiedAuthority gains purposes, and AuthorityError gains WidensPurposes; DTGCredentialError gains InvalidPurposes (non-exhaustive).

  • did:scid parties are matched by their DID. Chain verification (verify_chain, delegation chains) and the acknowledgement/acceptance pairing compare an issuer, subject, presenter, governing party or principal by DID, ignoring a did:scid ?src= locator (VTI-KEY-160): did:scid:vh:1:<scid>?src=a.example and did:scid:vh:1:<scid> are one party. A did:scid and its did:webvh log are still two. Every other DID compares as before. A proof's verificationMethod is still bound to its issuer exactly.

  • Depends on affinidi-did-common directly (already in the graph through affinidi-data-integrity).

Security

  • DTGCredential::verify_proof_with_public_key now refuses a proof that was not made by a key of the credential's issuer. It verified the signature under the key it was handed but never checked that the proof's verificationMethod belongs to issuer, so a caller that resolved the method the proof names and then trusted issuer() accepted a credential naming any issuer, signed by anyone. It now returns DTGCredentialError::ProofNotFromIssuer, as verify_grant_with_public_key already did; the two share one check. A method belongs to the issuer when the DID before its # is exactly the issuer, when it is the issuer itself, or when it is a bare #fragment (read against the issuer — verify_grant_with_public_key previously refused that form). The comparison is verbatim. A caller signing with a key whose id is not a method of the issuer will now see its own credentials refused; give the signing secret the issuer's method id.

title: ci(deps): bump the actions group with 2 updates
body:
Bumps the actions group with 2 updates: [korthout/backport-action](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action) and [taiki-e/install-action](https://github.com/taiki-e/install-action). Updates `korthout/backport-action` from 4.7.1 to 5.0.0
Release notes

Sourced from korthout/backport-action's releases.

Backport-action v5.0.0

🎂 Six years of backport-action

Six years ago today, on November 11, 2020, the first commit of backport-action landed. What started as a small script to save us from cherry-picking by hand has grown into an action trusted by projects of all sizes. Among the public repositories using it, 137 have over 100 stars, 67 have over 1,000, 18 have over 10,000, and 4 have over 100,000. We've had 48 releases, with contributions from 24 people. And we've collected 125 stars ourselves.

Thank you to everyone who contributed code, reported an issue, shared an idea, or simply trusted this action with your backports. A new major release is a fitting way to mark the occasion. Here's to the next six years!

Breaking changes

v5 is all about improving placeholders: the ${...} values the action fills into the pull_title, pull_description and branch_name templates. The default templates use them too. Most workflows won't notice a difference. If you've customized pull_title, pull_description or branch_name, check the notes below.

All placeholders

Every occurrence of a placeholder is replaced

A placeholder that occurs more than once in a template is now replaced everywhere. A template like ${pull_number} ... ${pull_number} now results in 123 ... 123, as you'd expect. Previously it resulted in 123 ... ${pull_number}.

The same fix also changes two less common cases:

  • Placeholders inside inserted text are no longer expanded. If the original pull request's description contains ${target_branch}, it now appears literally instead of being replaced.
  • $ in the original pull request's title or description is kept as written. Previously sequences like $$, $&, $` and $' were rewritten, so echo $$ > app.pid became echo $ > app.pid. If you worked around this, for example by doubling $$ into $$$$, remove the workaround.

Fixes #435 and #694.

  • Substitute placeholders in a single pass by @​korthout in korthout/backport-action#692

Specific placeholders

${issue_refs} lists the references a description refers to, once and as written, ignoring comments, code, and link text

${issue_refs} now reads the original pull request's description as Markdown and lists the issues and pull requests it refers to: each one once, as written there. It now ignores references in code, comments, and link text. In v4 it matched patterns in the raw text, so it missed many references and picked up some that weren't references at all.

Take this description:

Fixes [#752](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/752), fixes [#753](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/753). Follow-up of https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/pull/749
and [Korthout/Backport-Action#752](https://github.com/Korthout/Backport-Action/issues/752), see also [the checkout bug](https://github.com/actions/checkout/issues/1).

# not a reference: [#706](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/706)



<!-- Closes #755 -->

With pull_description: "Relates to ${issue_refs}", v4 gives Relates to [#706](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/706) [#755](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/755). v5 gives Relates to [Korthout/Backport-Action#752](https://github.com/Korthout/Backport-Action/issues/752) [#753](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/753) [korthout/backport-action#749](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/749) [actions/checkout#1](https://github.com/actions/checkout/issues/1).

  • Now listed: references next to punctuation, as in ([#123](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/123)) or Fixes [#123](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/123).; references separated by a single space; [GH-123](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/123); pull request URLs, also when followed by punctuation, a query or a fragment; and links to an issue or pull request, like [the bug](https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/123).
  • No longer listed: references in comments (<!-- ... -->), such as the instructions in a pull request template; in code (fenced, indented or inline); in HTML attributes or inside <code>, <pre> and <a href>; and in a link's text.
  • Each issue once, as written: a template could expand to [#1234](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/1234) [#1234](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/1234) [#1234](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/1234). Now each issue is listed once, in the order it first appears and in its first spelling. An issue written both as [#123](https://github.com/korthout/backport-action/issues/123) and in full is listed in full, so it keeps referring to the original repository.

title: chore(deps): Bump trust-tasks-build from 0.1.3 to 0.2.0
body:
Bumps [trust-tasks-build](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf) from 0.1.3 to 0.2.0.
Release notes

Sourced from trust-tasks-build's releases.

trust-tasks-build-v0.2.0

Added

  • rs,build: A generated file names the runtime contract it needs (#1253)

trust-tasks-rs gains a hidden __private::ABI_V1, and every file trust-tasks-build generates for an application opens with const _: () = ::trust_tasks_rs::__private::ABI_V1; under a comment naming the trust-tasks-build version. A runtime too old for the generator, or one that has moved to a newer contract, now fails on that line with an error naming the contract, instead of on whichever hidden door the generated code reaches first (#1101). The in-repo prebuilt tree is unchanged.

  • rs,build,ts,ts-gen,go,dart: Emit only the $defs each schema constant reaches (#1243)

  • feat(rs,build,ts,ts-gen,go,dart): emit only the $defs each schema constant reaches

    Each generated request and response schema constant now keeps only the root $defs its root reaches: the request drops Response and what only the response uses, the response document drops what only the request uses. Release notes

Sourced from affinidi-messaging-test-mediator's releases.

v0.51.0

Added — did:webs

  • The mediator resolves did:webs, so a did:webs client can authenticate and a did:webs recipient can be routed to. A did:webs resolves only when its KERI key event log verifies and the published did.json matches the verified key state, under the same default host policy as did:web and did:webvh: public hosts only, no redirects, no proxy. Requires affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.47, which does not turn on serde_json's preserve_order for the whole build. A mediator configured to resolve through a DID resolver cache server needs one that resolves did:webs (affinidi-did-resolver-cache-server 0.9.16).

Changed — container send-queue limits

  • The published container image now ships queued_send_messages_soft = 2000 and queued_send_messages_hard = 10000, matching the annotated template and the Rust defaults. It shipped 200 and 1000, so every deployment ran a send queue ten times tighter than the documented default while a code search reported 2000, which is a trap for anyone sizing a deployment or reading a queue_max_saturation_ratio against the wrong denominator. 200 is also tight in practice: a sender whose recipients stop deleting fills it in seconds. queued_receive_messages_soft and _hard are unchanged at 200 and 1000, because the receive limits bound total storage and the send limits do not; queued_send_messages_per_peer is unchanged at 50 and remains the gate that catches one sender flooding one recipient.

  • A standard account can no longer switch its own queue limit off. trust-tasks-rs-v0.39.0

Added

  • messaging/queue/purge: 0.1 gains storedBefore and selectedAt to pin a confirming purge to its dry run (#1288)
  • rooms/records/put: 0.6 declares a 2 MiB document bound (#1252)

  • feat(rooms/records/put): 0.6 declares a 64 KiB document bound

    rooms/records/put/0.6 extends 0.5 and changes no member. Its front matter declares maxDocumentBytes.request: 65536, the bound a deployed host already enforces, so hosts stop disagreeing on the largest record and a room can move between them without stranding records; larger content goes through files. Adding the bound to 0.5 in place would have narrowed what a 0.5 host must accept. The response declares no bound.

    Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart regenerated; earlier versions now carry "superseded by rooms/records/put/0.6".

  • rs,build: A generated file names the runtime contract it needs (#1253)

trust-tasks-rs gains a hidden __private::ABI_V1, and every file trust-tasks-build generates for an application opens with const _: () = ::trust_tasks_rs::__private::ABI_V1; under a comment naming the trust-tasks-build version. A runtime too old for the generator, or one that has moved to a newer contract, now fails on that line with an error naming the contract, instead of on whichever hidden door the generated code reaches first (#1101). The in-repo prebuilt tree is unchanged.

  • rs,https: Build the HTTPS server on consume_dispatched; async handlers and auth (#1244)

  • feat(rs,https)!: build the HTTPS server on consume_dispatched; async handlers and auth

    HttpsServer now runs every framework check through trust_tasks_rs::consume_dispatched_answer and keeps only the HTTP steps. The checks only it had become ConsumeChecks options (require_attribution, proof_did_methods, received_bytes). Adds on_async/on_ack_async, an AsyncAuth trait every Auth satisfies, extends forward routing with unsupportedVersion, and per-type maxDocumentBytes enforcement with a body limit derived from the registered tasks.

title: fix!: verify every VTA reply, and sign the TSP announce
body:
This is the app side of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1744. It follows two VTI changes:

- #1739: the VTA and the VTC accept a Trust Task over DIDComm or TSP only when its proof verifies as its `issuer`, and that issuer is the transport sender.
- #1740: every VTA and VTC response, errors included, is signed under `proofPurpose: authentication`.

## What the app sends

The app already sent only signed documents built by the engine: `whoami`, step-up approve/deny, task-consent approve/deny and `device/set-wake`, each with a fresh `urn:uuid` id, `issuedAt`, `issuer` set to the device `did:key` and `recipient` set to the VTA. With #1744 the engine:

- signs these under `authentication`, except the approver's own decisions: the step-up `approve-response` and the `task-consent/decision` (approve and deny for each). These are evidence the executor records, so they are signed under `assertionMethod`, and only with a key the device's `did:key` lists there;
- refuses to send any document that is unsigned, or is not issued by this holder to this VTA.

The one unsigned document was the TSP reachability announce, an unsigned `messaging/ping/0.1` that #1739 refuses. It is replaced by `VtaMobileAgent.announceTsp`, which sends a holder-signed ping. The engine's `announce` is removed.

The app sends none of the legacy DIDComm protocol messages that #1739 removes. It uses only the Trust Task envelope over DIDComm and the TSP binding envelope.

## Pushed approval requests

The step-up approve-request, consent request and task-consent request the VTA pushes are its operational messages. #1740 signs them with the operational key under `authentication`, and the #1744 engine refuses one signed under `assertionMethod`, or with a key the issuer does not list under `authentication`, before it prompts. The signed step-up fixtures in `AuthorizationContextTests` are re-signed under `authentication` with the same deterministic test key (seed 17). They were re-signed and checked with the engine's `verify_signed_request` in a throwaway Rust test.

## How replies are verified

| Transport | Where | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| DIDComm | engine, inside `MediatorSession.sendTrustTask` | proof by the VTA under `authentication` (key listed under `authentication`); `threadId` and `type` answer the request; issued by the VTA to this device |
| TSP | `TspReplyRouter.deliver`, via `verifyTrustTaskReply` | same, checked **before** the waiting `submit` is resolved |

Over TSP, a frame that echoes a `threadId` but fails verification is not consumed. The expectation stays open, so the genuine reply still resolves the submit, and a reply that never verifies times out. Error replies must verify too.

## Also

- Re-vendors `Sources/VtaMobileCore/VtaMobileCore.swift`, generated from the #1744 engine. The diff is large because the generator on main has moved on since the v0.6.17 release was vendored.
- The `Package.swift` pin TODO now points at #1744. Until a `vta-mobile-core-v*` release is cut from #1744 and the tag and checksum here are bumped, a checkout needs the local-xcframework override. **CI on this PR is expected to fail until then**: the v0.6.17 binary does not match the vendored bindings, and it still expects pushed requests under `assertionMethod`. No release is cut as part of this PR.
- The README and doc comments describe proof-bound requests and verified replies instead of intrinsic-sender auth, and the exception for the approver's decisions.

## Verification

No full Xcode is installed on the machine this was prepared on (Command Line Tools only), so `xcodebuild test` on a simulator and the XCTest suite were **not** run. What was run:

- `swiftc -typecheck` of `Sources/VtaMobileCore` and `Sources/VtaMobileAgent` against the regenerated bindings and FFI header (macOS target): clean.
- `App/` type-checked for Mac Catalyst (`arm64-apple-ios16.0-macabi`): clean apart from the `#Preview` macro, whose plugin ships only with Xcode.
- A throwaway macOS executable linking the host build of the #1744 engine, exercising the router and the real verifier. All checks passed:
  - a forged reply is not consumed, and the genuine reply resolves the waiter;
  - an unexpected thread passes through;
  - a reply that never verifies times out;
  - the engine refuses an unsigned reply with `UnverifiedReply`;
  - the default router does not consume an unsigned reply.
- The updated `TspReplyRouterTests`, including three new cases for these rules, and the re-signed `AuthorizationContextTests` fixtures were written but not compiled, since XCTest is unavailable here (`swiftc -parse` only).

Not run: an end-to-end test against a deployed VTA built from #1739 and #1740.

title: spec(vtc/rooms/community): a community-owned room states and changes its signal delay (create 0.5, update 0.4, get 0.5)
body:
A room a member owns states its signal delay at `rooms/create` 0.3, and its administrators change it at the host with `rooms/signal-delay/set` 0.1 (#1084). A room the **community** owns could do neither. The community is both the holder of `admin` and the host, and `vtc/rooms/community/create` and `update` had no field for it, so every community room waited a randomised few seconds before each `rooms/changed` signal, however its members used it. As a result, the VTC console can't offer the setting.

## What this adds
- **`vtc/rooms/community/create/0.5`**: an optional `signalDelay` (absent means `randomised`). It is recorded in the room's host record and always echoed back. A `none` create is audited along with the create.
- **`vtc/rooms/community/update/0.4`**: an optional `signalDelay`, applied together with the other details or not at all.
  - Changing only the delay counts as a change: it is audited, and `detailsUpdatedAt` and `detailsUpdatedBy` move. It needs no profile write.
  - It touches no watch.
  - Updating the host record is now allowed for this one field.
- **`vtc/rooms/community/get/0.5`**: always returns the room's `signalDelay`.
- **Refusal on both writes:** `signalDelayNotPermitted` when the community's governance as host keeps the delay for every room. Nothing in the request is applied.
- **Surfaces:** a surface that offers `none` SHOULD say what it gives up.

Links to create 0.4, update 0.3 and get 0.4 have moved to the new versions (`npm run fix-stale-references`).

## Checks run
- Rust, TS, Go and Dart libraries regenerated.
- Passed: `npm run check`, `check-bindings`, `build`, `build-bundles` + `check-bundles`, and the `trust-tasks-rs` conformance tests (4104 passed).

Consumer: VTI (the VTC console's create form gets the setting, and a community room's page can edit it).

title: feat(vtc): a community room's signal delay is chosen at creation and changed on its page (create 0.5, update 0.4, get 0.5)
body:
Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1336.

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1336 is merged and published; `vti-specs-vtc` pins the three new versions from trusttasks.org.

## Why
A room the community owns was always created with the randomised watch-signal delay, and nothing could change it.
- `vtc/rooms/community/create` and `update` had no `signalDelay`.
- `rooms/signal-delay/set` is sent to a room's host by a holder of its `admin`, and for a community room both of those are the community itself.

So the console had nothing to offer.

## What changes
- **vtc-service** serves create 0.5, update 0.4 and get 0.5 beside the older versions (create 0.4, update 0.3, get 0.3/0.4).
  - The delay is stored in the room's host record (`vti_rooms::Room::signal_delay`), which the watcher reads each time it fires.
  - Update writes the host record first, then the owner's record, and puts the host record back if the owner's write fails.
  - Changing only the delay counts as a `detailsUpdated` change, audited with the old and new values. It needs no profile write.
  - A create with `none` is audited along with the create.
  - The community accepts either setting, so `signalDelayNotPermitted` can't be emitted. It is listed in the error-code census baseline.
- **Console**
  - **New community room** and **Edit details** get a *Watch signals* choice: after a short random wait (the default) or at once. Choosing *at once* shows what it gives up before anything is sent.
  - The room's page shows the current setting.
  - The host's page for a community-owned room now points to Community rooms instead of `pnm`.
- **cnm**: `rooms create|update --signal-delay randomised|none`, with the same warning before it sends `none`.
- **vtc-mcp**: `room_open` creates at 0.5.
- **vta-sdk**: OpenAPI wrappers for the three new versions. The old wrappers are kept, since removing one is a breaking change.
- **Docs**: `community-rooms.md` has a new *Watch signals* section; `data-rooms.md` is updated.

## Tests
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7701 passed.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: everything passed except 7 tests on the first run.
  - 6 of them check the embedded admin-UI bundle and fail whenever the run uses `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1`.
  - The 7th was a real omission (`get/0.5` missing from the proof-requirement allowlist), now fixed.
  - All 7 pass on a re-run with the UI built.
- Doctests, `clippy -D warnings`, `fmt --check` and `check-docs.py` pass.
- Console: `npm run lint`; vitest for the plugins passes 640 tests, then 58 in the two rooms files after the new tests were added.
- New tests:
  - Integration test `vtc_rooms_community_signal_delay_is_set_at_create_read_and_changed`.
  - Conformance entries for the three new versions.
  - Console tests for the create toggle, the edit toggle and `detailsUpdate`.
  - A cnm payload test.

title: Harden VDC chains and bind VDC/VAC invocations to their request
body:
Prompted by a side-by-side comparison of the VDC and VAC with [ZCAP-LD v0.4.0](https://w3c-ccg.github.io/zcap-spec/v0.4.0/). The comparison found several places where the VDC's chain rules were implied rather than stated, one gap that is exploitable, and one place where both credentials trail ZCAP: what an invocation must be bound to. The changes tighten those without touching what the VDC is for: single hop by default, required acceptance, offline verification, a minimal ZK-friendly schema, and governance-owned scope vocabularies.

### VDC (`spec/body.md`)
- **Issuer binding (security fix).** A derived VDC's `issuer` MUST be its parent's `credentialSubject.id`. Rules 1–5 never said who may derive a link, so anyone holding a copy of a grant with `maxDepth` ≥ 1 could issue a child under it and have a party of their choosing (possibly themselves) accept it. The VAC already has this rule (Security Considerations item 16).
- **An acceptance on every link.** Every grant in a chain must come with its acceptance, not only the leaf.
- **Chain presentation becomes MUST.** The holder presents every grant and acceptance up to the root, and a verifier rejects a chain it cannot complete from the presentation. This matches the VAC. It discloses nothing new, since the verifier needed the chain anyway.
- **Depth ceiling of 8 grants.** The verifier enforces this regardless of `maxDepth`, which is set by the issuer and so does not protect the verifier from denial of service. The number is the same as the VAC's.
- **Per-level limits stated.** Each link may lower `maxDepth` for its own delegate, or omit it to end the chain. No link may raise it.
- **`redelegable` (new, OPTIONAL).** A subset of `scope` that the delegate may pass on. Example: book yourself, but only hand off search. It uses exact matching, like `scope`. It needs a context term, so an editor's note in Context Versions says issuers MUST NOT emit it until the next context version is recorded.
- **An edge needs both halves.** The edge's effective validity ends at the earlier `validUntil` of the grant and the acceptance, and revoking either half withdraws it. This gives a delegate a way to resign.
- **Withdrawal cascades.** Stated explicitly, together with the exposure when status is absent, mirroring the VAC's Withdrawal section.

### VDC and VAC
- **Invocation binding minimum.** A demonstration of key control MUST be fresh (a verifier challenge, or a nonce within a governance-defined window), MUST name its verifier, MUST name the act, and MUST be bound to the digest of the credential. How it is carried stays with the Trust Tasks spec, which may choose how but not whether. The VAC references the VDC's list, and its "no `audience` field" reasoning is kept: the verifier is named in the demonstration, not in the credential.
- **Security Considerations.** Items 12, 14 and 21 are extended rather than adding new items, so existing item numbers stay the same.
- **Relationship to Capability Models.** "Mappings … left to future work" is replaced with an informative ZCAP-LD ↔ VAC ↔ VDC correspondence table.

### `CONTEXT.md`
- VDC entry updated.

### Not changed, deliberately
- Open re-delegation by default, caveats, URL target narrowing, and optional acceptance. Each would weaken the principal's register of who may act in its name, consent, or ZK-friendliness.
- Salting `parent`/`accepts`. This is handled across all credentials by #87.

### Follow-ups
- Registry: add `redelegable` under `delegation` in the next context version (alongside #87's `v3`, if that is still open). Then drop the editor's note.
- Trust Tasks: carry the four invocation properties in the delegated and authority invocation protocols.

Rendered with `npm run render`. The only warning (dangling definitions) was already present on `main`.

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  the commit subjects.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `verify-go` builds, vets and tests, then `publish-go` pushes the
  tag, which *is* the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `verify-dart` checks each package against the *published* core,
  `tag-dart` pushes the tag, and `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

Every bump follows the commit subjects; an undeclared API break is refused on its
pull request by that language's API compatibility check (`rs`, `ts`, `go` and
`Dart API compatibility`).

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

[Python] Release 0.61.2

title: spec(vtc/rooms/community): a community-owned room states and changes its signal delay (create 0.5, update 0.4, get 0.5) (#1336)
body:
spec(vtc/rooms/community): a community-owned room states and changes its signal delay (create 0.5, update 0.4, get 0.5) (#1336)

A room a member owns states its signal delay at rooms/create 0.3 and its
administrators change it at the host with rooms/signal-delay/set 0.1. A
room the community owns could do neither: the community is both the
holder of `admin` and the host, and vtc/rooms/community/create and
update carried no such member, so every community room waited a
randomised few seconds before each rooms/changed signal however its
members used it.

- create 0.5 takes an optional `signalDelay` (absent = randomised),
  records it in the room's host record and always echoes it. A `none`
  create is audited with the create.
- update 0.4 takes an optional `signalDelay`, applied to the host record
  with the other details, together or not at all; a change of the delay
  alone is a change (audited, details timestamps move) that needs no
  profile write. It touches no watch.
- get 0.5 always serves the room's `signalDelay`.
- Both writes refuse `signalDelayNotPermitted` when the community's
  governance as host keeps the delay everywhere, applying nothing.
- A surface offering `none` SHOULD say what it gives up.

Links to create 0.4, update 0.3 and get 0.4 move to the new versions.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: Guide: formal verification review, run 3 — record 025 reworked after the cryptographic review
body:
Updates the *Formal verification review* chapter for run 3, the companion of [dtgwg-zkp-spec #26](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-zkp-spec/pull/26).

- **Run register**: row 3 (evidence [`7cc658e`](https://github.com/mitchuski/dtgwg-zkp-mage/commit/7cc658e89c8f), 19 records, 70 clauses, 79 roots, 37 review-witness theorems, sealed root `sha256:6e963611…`).
- **Run 3 section**: the cryptographic review filed as dtgwg-zkp-spec #25 found that record 025's relation was sound and did not meet the record's stated need; the model is rebuilt; building the circuit then found that a pre-rotation digest over the whole next leaf cannot be minted.
- **Findings F10 to F13**, a note on F9, and one new candidate for formal work: stating a record's need as a theorem.

Render and `npm run check` pass. Merge after #26, since the chapter cites the evidence revision that PR pins.

title: Cryptographic review of 18 November folded: record 025 reworked, records 007, 009, 022, 024 amended
body:
Folds the cryptographic review of records 007, 009, 022, 024 and 025 (#25). Every point is taken. Record 025 moves to `constructed` (second commit); no other record changes state. Evidence revision pinned in Appendix B: [`7cc658e`](https://github.com/mitchuski/dtgwg-zkp-mage/commit/7cc658e89c8f).

### Record 025 — reworked

As first specified the rotation proof needed the current secret, so a lost secret could not be replaced although the record's stated need covers loss; and the replacement leaf took a fresh revocation handle, so a member could rotate out of reach of revocation.

- The enrolment leaf is `Com(H(s), N, ρ; r)`: the image of the presenting secret, the pre-rotation digest `N = Hpre(H(s′))`, the revocation handle.
- Clauses 3 and 4: the rotation is authorised by the pre-committed next secret `s′`, which opens `L′`. The retiring leaf is opened by `H(s)`, so `s` is not a witness. A lost `s` rotates; a stolen `s` alone cannot.
- Clause 5 (new, record 009): `L′` carries the same handle `ρ`, proven equal without disclosing it. Revocation survives the rotation.
- The spent-tag set is committed over strictly sorted tags, as record 006 requires of `rl_root`; records 010, 023 and 024 name `spent_root` as a public input.
- Formal model rebuilt: `next_secret_fixed`, `handle_carried_forward`, `revocation_survives_rotation`, and `fresh_handle_escapes` as the counter-deployment for the earlier relation. Knowledge of `s′` is knowledge soundness and stays outside the model.

### Second commit — the circuit, and what building it found

- The rotation is built in the evidence repository: `runtimes/circom-gadget/circuits/rotation.circom`, one circuit, 11,987 constraints, six public signals, about 1.3 s to prove and 21 ms to verify, 320 B with compressed points; lab-only setup. Thirteen fixtures pass, among them: a witness built with no presenting secret among the inputs; a stolen presenting secret that cannot rotate; a replacement under another handle refused; a member revoked after rotating who cannot rotate again.
- Building it corrected clause 3. The first commit kept the pre-rotation digest over the whole next leaf, `N = H(L′)`. That leaf carries its own digest over the leaf after it, so the first leaf can never be minted. The digest now commits to the next secret's image, as a key event log commits to the next key, and the replacement leaf is minted at the rotation.
- Record 006's sorted-neighbour clause gets its first runtime, as a template in the same circuit: range leaves, one inclusion proof, two 128-bit comparisons. One fixture commits an unsorted list and shows a revoked handle passing, which is the registry's duty the proof cannot check.
- Not built: the presentation side of a rotation-capable profile (the tag-absence clause against `spent_root`).

### Records 007, 009, 022, 024 — amended

- **007**: the quantum-confidentiality line corrected (a hash commitment is computationally hiding; a SNARK-native key gives up `s` to Shor); salt distinctness and hardened derivation at issuance; knowledge of an opening separated from control of the DID.
- **009**: canonical form and injective encoding of the compared value; verification under a hidden issuer recorded as an open requirement of records 020 and 021 (one line each); the colluding-issuer claim narrowed.
- **022**: the relation restated for the adopted in-credential salt, `H(JCS(credential incl. salt))`; mandatory disclosure of the salt under selective-disclosure suites found to reopen the enumeration (raised on cred-spec PR #87); in-circuit JSON reading named as a risk.
- **024**: the anonymity claim stated over the non-colluding vetters; a stated policy and a k − 1 reading for self-attestation in the Groth16 route; option 1's assumptions; a profile's setup requirement.
- **007, 009, 022** and Public Input Conventions: the transcript binding is record 003's clause; a declared but unconstrained `transcriptDigest` is not bound.

### Chapters

Integration (rotation under the identifier commitment profile, WG-17), Security Considerations (trusted setup), Appendix D changelog, the WG-15 and WG-17 rows.

### Checks

`validate` 24/24, `test` pass, render clean. Formal gate in the evidence repository: 19 records, 70 clauses, 79 roots and 37 review-witness theorems within the standard axioms, `leanchecker --fresh` clean; sealed root `sha256:6e963611fcdd91dfc0e2f1ec6f6ad8e3d70b2f9cd07e404bb8bef6e95eb6464d`. Circuit: `node test-rotation.mjs`, 13/13.

### Open for a second reading (WG-17)

- Custody of the rotation material: `s′` and the opening of `L` kept apart from `s`, or all of it derived from `s′`.
- Whether the rotation tag should key on `H(s)` as written.

Answers #25, which stays open for the reviewer's second reading of 025.

title: Salt every DTG credential so digest references cannot be enumerated
body:
Closes #38.

Implements the placement agreed on #38 (stormer78's 25 Sep proposal, +1 from bmiller59, matching ZKP record 022): one top-level `salt` inside every credential's hashed block, so every digest that references the credential is blinded at once.

### Changes (`spec/body.md`)
- **Base Structure:** new `salt` member: REQUIRED under context `v3` and later, absent under `v1`/`v2`; exactly 32 bytes from a CSPRNG, fresh per credential, never reused or derived, base-58-btc multibase. Kept on re-proof, redrawn on re-issue. Mandatory-disclosure under selective-disclosure suites. Verifiers reject a `v3` credential with a missing or malformed salt. The `@context` bullet now admits later context versions (it already had to, for `v2`).
- **Context Versions:** `v3` = `v2` + `salt`; once its digest is recorded, every credential lists `v3` or later. Editor's note (same pattern as #84): `v3` isn't published yet, so issuers MUST NOT emit `salt` until it is, and examples move to `v3` when the digest is recorded.
- **Digest Encoding:** the "none of these is salted" editor's note becomes a **Salting** subsection: why, a salted grant + acknowledgement example whose `digestMultibase` reproduces from the grant as printed (and the unsalted digest for contrast), and what a salt does *not* do: presentation linkability, `taskDigestMultibase` (going away under #58), and VSC `predicate` blinding stay with ZKP work. Profile-defined digests: SHOULD reference something salted or say why enumeration isn't a concern.
- **Vetting profile** and the **ZK editor's note** updated to point at the new subsection.
- **`CONTEXT.md`:** Salt entry.

### Follow-ups
- **Registry:** `dtgwg-vsc-registry` needs a `v3` context (= `v2` + a plain-string `salt` term) per GOVERNANCE §3.1; then a small PR records the digest, drops the editor's note and moves the examples to `v3` with salts (several example digests will change then).
- **`nodeType` (#53)** could join `v3` if its value list is settled first.
- No Document Status bump here; leaving that for the release that records `v3`.

Rendered with `npm run render`: no errors, and all in-page links resolve.

title: docs(adoption): add first-use RAHP specification tutorial
body:
Closes #49

## What changed

Adds a consumer-facing, step-by-step tutorial over the existing retained-source TRQP examination. The tutorial shows the complete upstream sequence from bounded assurance question through affected contexts, source pinning, local risk hypotheses, replay observations, review/evidence binding, validation, fail-closed behavior, interpretation and reassessment.

It does not introduce a new review contract, canonical risks, downstream pressure-test semantics or an assurance decision engine.

## Artefact IDs affected

None. No canonical `data/` or `method/` records are changed.

Documentation and regression coverage only:

- `review/examples/standalone-trqp/TUTORIAL.md` (new)
- `tests/test_first_use_tutorial.py` (new)
- `README.md` (first-use navigation)
- `review/examples/standalone-trqp/README.md` (navigation/accuracy)
- `ADOPTION.md` (first-use route)

## Provenance — what triggered this change?

Issue #49. The existing upstream retained-source TRQP example is technically complete enough to reproduce, but its README primarily serves as a technical reference. The downstream RAHP Toolkit demonstrated the value of a sequential worked example. This contribution adapts that usability lesson to the canonical upstream review/evidence contracts without importing downstream-only schemas, identifiers or controller semantics.

The tutorial was substantially AI-assisted and then checked against the current upstream files, validators, retained outputs and contribution guidance. Independent human review remains required.

## Validation output

The PR workflow completed successfully. The added regression executed the documented replay, review validation, composed examination and deliberate mutable-revision failure.

```
PASS · 43 RK · 66 CT · 21 GR · 21 AT · 37 M · 36 US · 33 SC · 21 EPIC · 16 PERSONA · 9 REC · 3 RA · 3 GP · 0 errors · 32 warnings
```

The 32 retained corpus warnings are the existing task-force work queue and are not introduced by this documentation tranche.

## Assurance and compatibility

- The retained TRQP source, review record, evidence sidecar, risk source and replay implementation are unchanged.
- No schema, vocabulary, corpus, API or governance semantics change.
- Documentation explicitly separates machine validity, evidence integrity, reviewer inference, assurance judgment and governance authority.
- A successful replay remains `overall_assurance: review-required`.
- The tutorial includes affected people/contexts and plausible harm before risk selection.
- The negative exercise uses the repository's existing invalid mutable-revision fixture.
- Local-link and command regression coverage is intended to prevent obvious documentation drift.

## Out of scope / residual evidence

- No claim of TRQP deployment assurance or full conformance.
- No risk scoring, risk acceptance or governance decision.
- No general evidence-sidecar standardization.
- No downstream CRK mappings, portable-pattern identifiers, pressure-test controller or rendered-output machinery.
- Independent methodological review is still required.

## Checklist

- [x] `python3 tools/validate.py` exits 0
- [x] Every new/changed record has a `provenance` block (not applicable: no canonical records changed)
- [x] New guardrails have an assurance test; new controls reach a metric (not applicable)
- [x] No generated file under `build/` was edited by hand
- [x] If a risk score changed, the evidence for the change is stated above (not applicable)
- [x] DCO/CLA and required CI checks pass on the current head
- [ ] Independent review complete


### First-use review response (11 November 2026)

title: Let a provisioner create contexts beneath its own without administrat…
body:
…ive authority: the additive context-create capability (VTI-CTX-026 – VTI-CTX-028)

A process that mints a context for each software agent it manages sits on a host that faces the network, so it should not hold the administrative role: an administrator of a context can write access control entries for it, and a compromise of the process would then rewrite everything it created. Creating a context is the one power it needs.

VTI-CTX-020 already requires act authority covering the parent, and VTI-ACL-033 already defines an additive capability, so this adds no new mechanism. It registers one capability and states what it confers:

- VTI-CTX-026: an entry holding `context-create` may create a context beneath one its act scope covers, whatever its role, meeting the same creation requirements as any other creator.
- VTI-CTX-027: it never permits a root context or one outside the entry's act scope, confers nothing else, and writes no access control entry for the creator, so authority cannot accumulate one context at a time. Consistent with VTI-VTA-032.
- VTI-CTX-028: it may name a covered context's primary DID, only while that context has none and only to an identifier the context's own keys control; changing or clearing it stays an administrator's act. A context with no identity can be issued as nothing, so without this a creator would need an administrator to finish every context it makes.

Appendix C.2 gains the `context-create` row and the reason it is additive.

The alternative considered, a separate always-available service holding unrestricted act authority that creates contexts on callers' behalf, is recorded in the rationale and rejected: it is a new component whose only purpose is to hold the most powerful grant in the system.

This is a change proposal against the requirements. It is deliberately not a divergence-register entry, and records nothing about any implementation.

title: fix(vtc): a member can add a passkey with a hardware key when their DID is long
body:
Hi Glenn,

Thanks for all the work on VTI. I ran into a bug while adding a passkey in the member portal, and this started as my attempt at a small fix. It now includes your follow-up commits (a708b13ba, 55327b668).

## The problem

On the member portal, adding a passkey with a YubiKey failed with "Passkey creation was cancelled". The PIN was accepted, but the touch prompt never appeared. The same key worked on other VTCs.

The cause is the name we send to the authenticator. `register_start` passes the member's whole DID as WebAuthn `user.name` and `user.displayName`. A `did:webvh` is about 95 bytes, and this key rejects a `user.name` longer than 64 bytes. CTAP2 only requires authenticators to accept 64. The key answers `CTAP1_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH` before asking for a touch, and Chrome turns any such CTAP error into a generic `NotAllowedError`, which is where the "cancelled" message comes from.

## How I checked

I took the exact options the portal returns and ran them against the key directly (python-fido2) and through `navigator.credentials.create` in Chrome. Only the name changed between runs:

| `user.name` | CTAP result | Chrome |
|---|---|---|
| 95 bytes (the DID) | `INVALID_LENGTH` (0x03), no touch prompt | `NotAllowedError` |
| 64 bytes | OK | not run |
| 65 bytes | `INVALID_LENGTH` | not run |
| 59 bytes (output of the original version of this PR) | OK | OK |

A long `displayName` on its own was accepted; only `user.name` is limited. PIN, `credProtect`, `userVerification: required` and the algorithm list were identical in every run.

Environment: YubiKey 5 series, firmware 5.7.4, Chrome 156 on Linux. I only tried this one key, so other keys may behave differently.

## The change (current head)

- `vti_common::auth::passkey::AuthenticatorName` is the only way to build a name for an authenticator (`for_did`, `from_label`, `for_did_or_label`), and it is bounded to 64 **bytes**. `vti_common::auth::passkey::start_passkey_registration` is the one place a registration starts. The VTC wrapper, the three VTC DID-named paths (member portal, admin passkeys, step-up redeem), the VTC install ceremony and the VTA passkey-VM enrolment all go through it.
- Naming rules:
  - `did:webvh` / `did:tdw`: `<host:path> (<last 6 chars of SCID>)`, e.g. `dids.example.org:example-member-000001 (000000)`. If host+path doesn't fit it keeps both ends joined by `…`.
  - Any other DID: unchanged if 64 bytes or less, otherwise first 40 bytes + `…` + last 21 bytes.
  - VTA operator-supplied label: used as given; if over 64 bytes, `…` plus its tail.
  - All cuts are on char boundaries. The same name is applied to `user.name` and `user.displayName`.
- The VTA's old `display_name_for` is removed. It capped at 64 characters, not bytes, and its long branch produced 66 bytes, so it had the same bug.
- The private copy of `authenticator_name` in `step_up_passkey.rs` is removed.

The name is display only. The account is still identified by `user.id` and this service's own record, as before.

Behaviour changes to be aware of: a webvh name now carries a SCID fragment and shows host+path rather than the first-40/last-16 form, so names differ from what the step-up flow showed before, and from what the VTA produced.

## Testing

- CI is green on the current head.
- Glenn reports vtc-service + vtc-client 3598/3598, vti-common and vta-service passkey tests, workspace clippy `-D warnings` and doc tests all passing locally.
- YubiKey check on the current head (55327b668): I ran a local test VTC built from this head and added a passkey from Chrome with the same YubiKey. It worked: the touch prompt appeared and the passkey registered. The server returned `user.name` and `user.displayName` of `first.example.com:members:alice (2bwPSE)` (40 bytes) for an 88-byte `did:webvh`, where the original code sent all 88. This used the repo's `TestVtc` harness with a wallet-proven member session, not the real wallet sign-in, and not a deployed community portal.
- I have **not** run it against a deployed portal such as the one where I first hit the bug; that is still open.
- Test gaps I'd like covered (also requested in my comment above): `did:webvh:<scid>:` with an empty tail and `did:webvh:<scid>` with no colon; host+path of exactly 64 and 65 bytes; exact-output assertions for 2-byte and 3-byte characters; and one test that the options returned by the three DID-named call sites carry the short name.

## Open questions

- Over-length webvh with a long host: the host head is capped at about 26 bytes, so hosts longer than that are cut inside the host. Is that acceptable?
- An over-long VTA `label` keeps its tail; for free text, keeping the head may read better.

Thanks for taking a look.

Brendan

title: fix(vtc): a member can add a passkey with a hardware key when their DID is long (#2453)
body:
fix(vtc): a member can add a passkey with a hardware key when their DID is long (#2453)

* fix(vtc): a member can add a passkey with a hardware key when their DID is long

Adding a passkey in the member portal failed on a YubiKey 5 (firmware
5.7.4) with "Passkey creation was cancelled": the key answered
CTAP1_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH to the registration, after the PIN and before
any touch prompt, and Chrome reports every such CTAP error as a generic
NotAllowedError.

The portal sent the member's whole DID as WebAuthn user.name and
user.displayName. A did:webvh is ~95 bytes, and the key rejects a
user.name over 64 bytes (CTAP2 only requires authenticators to accept
64). Tried against the key, with only the name changed: 64 bytes passes,
65 fails, and a long displayName on its own is accepted.

The step-up enrolment flow already shortened a long DID to its two ends
(authenticator_name), but the member portal and the admin passkey paths
call start_passkey_registration directly and did not. Move that helper
into the shared start_passkey_registration wrapper so every registration
shows the same short name, count it in bytes rather than characters so a
multi-byte DID cannot pass 64 bytes, and drop the private copy in
step_up_passkey.

The name is display only; the account is identified by user.id and this
service's own record, as before. A DID of 64 bytes or less is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Brendan A. Miller <code+os@brendanmiller.com>

* fix(passkey): one byte-bounded authenticator name for the VTA and the VTC

The VTA's passkey-VM enrolment had the same defect this PR fixes in the
VTC: `display_name_for` capped the name at 64 characters, not bytes, and
its long branch emitted `…` plus 63 characters, 66 bytes even for ASCII,
so a YubiKey 5 refuses `vta/passkey-vms/*` enrolment for a long webvh
path or operator label. The two services kept separate copies of the
rule, which is how they drifted.

Move the rule to `vti_common::auth::passkey`, beside `build_webauthn`:
`MAX_AUTHENTICATOR_NAME_BYTES`, `authenticator_name_for_did` and
`clamp_authenticator_name`. A did:webvh is named by its host and path
(its SCID is unreadable and the head of the DID is almost all SCID);
other long DIDs keep their two ends. The VTC wrapper now only enforces
the byte limit, and its DID-named callers pass
`authenticator_name_for_did`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(passkey): one AuthenticatorName type and one registration start for the VTA and the VTC

Review follow-up on the byte-bounded authenticator name.

- `vti_common::auth::passkey::AuthenticatorName` replaces the free
  `authenticator_name_for_did` / `clamp_authenticator_name`. It is only
  built by `for_did`, `from_label` or `for_did_or_label`, so a name over
  64 bytes cannot reach an authenticator, and a caller can no longer pass
  a raw DID by mistake (the test fixtures did, and so exercised naming
  production never used).
- `vti_common::auth::passkey::start_passkey_registration` is the one
  place both services start a registration: the VTA's passkey-VM
  enrolment, the VTC wrapper (which adds EdDSA on top) and the VTC install
  ceremony. The bound is no longer enforced twice in the VTC and separately
  in the VTA.
- `did:tdw` (webvh's earlier name) is named like `did:webvh`, as the VTA's
  old `display_name_for` did for any SCID-first method.
- A webvh name ends with the SCID's last six characters,
  `dids.example.org:persona (wUF4kX)`, so two DIDs re-created at one path
  are told apart in the picker.
- A webvh host and path too long to fit keep both ends, so the host stays
  visible rather than only the path's tail.
- Uses std's `floor_char_boundary` / `ceil_char_boundary` (MSRV 1.95).
- The naming tests live with the type and check every cut is a true head
  and tail of its source, so a split character fails them.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

Changelog

## `vta-signing`

## [0.1.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/releases/tag/vta-signing-v0.1.0) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vta-signing**: A small signing library the VTA and its callers share ([#2745](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2745)) * feat(keys): keys/sign-jws/0.1 — a VTA-built compact JWS walled off to JWT types Add a `keys/sign-jws/0.1` Trust Task that produces a compact JWS (a JWT) over a caller-supplied JOSE header and claims set, signed by a stored key. Unlike `keys/sign/0.1` it is not a general signing oracle: the VTA assembles the `b64url(header).b64url(payload)` signing input itself and signs it under `SigningDomain::ProtocolDefined`, so the result verifies as a JWS rather than as a VTA opaque-signing payload. The task is walled off so it can never be pointed at producing a credential or issuer artifact: - the finalized protected header's `typ` must be on a small allow-list of JWT profiles (`JWT`, `at+jwt`, `oauth-id-jag+jwt`, `dpop+jwt`, `logout+jwt`); anything else — e.g. a Verifiable Credential media type — is refused before the key is touched; - the VTA, not the caller, sets `alg` from the key, so a caller cannot request a signature under an algorithm the key does not implement or mislabel one; - the payload must be a JSON object (a JWT claims set); raw bytes still go through the opaque oracle, not here. Authorized exactly as `keys/sign` is — per the key's context — so the same context separation that walls off a signer's identities applies. Added to the dispatch table with the spec's (none / none / actsAsSubject) class, and acknowledged in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` pending an upstream spec in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf (dispatched unvalidated like any unknown-schema task until then). Enables the Agent Gateway to delegate JWT signing (STS access tokens, ID-JAG) to the VTA while keeping the JWT-signing path structurally separate from credential signing.
## `vti-specs-vta`
## [0.11.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-specs-vta-v0.10.0...vti-specs-vta-v0.11.0) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vta**: Every DID the VTA holds through one method-neutral surface (vta/dids/*) ([#2763](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2763)) * feat(vta)!: every DID the VTA holds through one method-neutral surface (vta/dids/*)
## `vti-specs-vtc`
## [0.7.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vti-specs-vtc-v0.7.0...vti-specs-vtc-v0.7.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vtc-service**: Serve vtc/storage/credentials/recipient/0.1 so the console seals for any DID method ([#2762](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2762)) * feat(vtc-service): serve vtc/storage/credentials/recipient/0.1 so the console seals for any DID method The console sealed a storage credential to the key it read from the community's same-origin /.well-known/did.jsonl. A did:webs community serves no log, so sealing always failed and the console fell back to `cnm`. A did:webvh community on a DID host failed the same way. The community now answers vtc/storage/credentials/recipient/0.1 (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1329): - It returns the Ed25519 key it opens sealed blocks with, as a did:key, plus the verification method that publishes it (item 2). - When its own DID resolves, the answer is checked against that document. If the document publishes a different signing key, the answer is `notPublished` (retryable) and carries no key, so nothing is sealed to a key that has rotated away (item 3). - It requires `vtc.rooms.admin`, the same authority as credentials/set (item 1). The console asks this task instead of reading did.jsonl. It accepts the answer only when it names the community's own DID (item 4) and seals to it as given (item 5). - **vtc-service**: Store and serve an uploaded community logo ([#2751](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2751)) * feat(vtc-service): store and serve an uploaded community logo A community can now upload its logo, and the VTC serves it from its own origin, so it shows in the console, the member portal, both sign-in pages and the default landing page wherever the VTC is hosted. Before this, the logo was only the profile's `logoUrl`. Those pages are served with `img-src 'self' data:`, so a logo at any other address was never drawn, and a deployment with nowhere on the VTC's own origin to put a file (a hosted VTC, say) had no logo at all: a filesystem website must have its own host, and `admin_ui.members_dir` is a snapshot that stops following the daemon on every upgrade. Served from memory against a small record read, with a fixed `Content-Type`, `nosniff`, `default-src 'none'; sandbox`, an `ETag` and `304`. Bytes that do not match their record are never served. - A `logo` member (`url`, `sha256`, `mediaType`, `width`, `height`) on the public profile and on `/v1/member/me`'s `community`. Every page draws it in preference to `logoUrl`, which is unchanged. - Console: a Logo card on the Community profile page. It rasterizes an SVG in the browser, from a `data:` URL inside an `` where it runs no script, so no SVG is ever sent or stored. The Logo URL field now says when these pages will not draw the address it holds. Design note: docs/05-design-notes/vtc-community-logo.md.

## `vta-keys`
## [0.44.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-keys-v0.44.0...vta-keys-v0.44.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vta-signing**: A small signing library the VTA and its callers share ([#2745](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2745)) * feat(keys): keys/sign-jws/0.1 — a VTA-built compact JWS walled off to JWT types Add a `keys/sign-jws/0.1` Trust Task that produces a compact JWS (a JWT) over a caller-supplied JOSE header and claims set, signed by a stored key. Unlike `keys/sign/0.1` it is not a general signing oracle: the VTA assembles the `b64url(header).b64url(payload)` signing input itself and signs it under `SigningDomain::ProtocolDefined`, so the result verifies as a JWS rather than as a VTA opaque-signing payload. The task is walled off so it can never be pointed at producing a credential or issuer artifact: - the finalized protected header's `typ` must be on a small allow-list of JWT profiles (`JWT`, `at+jwt`, `oauth-id-jag+jwt`, `dpop+jwt`, `logout+jwt`); anything else — e.g. a Verifiable Credential media type — is refused before the key is touched; - the VTA, not the caller, sets `alg` from the key, so a caller cannot request a signature under an algorithm the key does not implement or mislabel one; - the payload must be a JSON object (a JWT claims set); raw bytes still go through the opaque oracle, not here. Authorized exactly as `keys/sign` is — per the key's context — so the same context separation that walls off a signer's identities applies. Added to the dispatch table with the spec's (none / none / actsAsSubject) class, and acknowledged in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` pending an upstream spec in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf (dispatched unvalidated like any unknown-schema task until then). A did:webs host serves the array form, so a did:webs VTA's readiness gate could not resolve its own DID (DocumentMismatch: "did.json's services differ from those the stream authorises") and never connected to its mediator. 0.13.9 compares types as a set (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#1173). - Workspace lockfile: affinidi-did-webs 0.13.4 -> 0.13.9 (with affinidi-did-common 0.4.10, affinidi-crypto 0.3.4). - Enclave proxy lockfile: 0.13.3 -> 0.13.9. It also leaves affinidi-crypto 0.2 (secrets-resolver 0.5.21, data-integrity 0.8.11, did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.57, rdf-encoding 0.1.11), so one crypto version remains and it builds. - vta-keys: a test moves from the deprecated `affinidi_crypto::p256::verify` to `verify_signature` (deprecated in affinidi-crypto 0.3.4).
## `vta-service`

Two places assumed one signing key per identity: - vault/sign-trust-task signed every document with the entry's one stored signingKeyId. A wallet sign-in signs auth/oob/identify for authentication and auth/oob/grant for assertionMethod, so a community refused one of the two whichever key the entry named (VTI-KEY-022). Where the principal is a key-role did:webs this agent holds, the purpose now decides the key; every other principal still signs with the entry's key. The key is still held to the entry's context (custody rule 7). - vta/dids/list reported the key event log's key as signingKeyId, which a client then stored in the entry: a method the document lists nowhere. It now reports the operational key for a key-role identity. persona_key_for also answers for a key-role did:webs, with the role key of the relationship, checked against the identity's own document and held to the same record checks as a level-1 identity. - **vta-service**: Refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:w… ([#2765](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2765)) * fix(vta-service): refuse to sign a document as the did:key of a did:webvh update key A VTA-built did:webvh uses one key as its signing key and its log's update key. keys/sign-document signed a caller's document as the did:key of any key in the caller's scope, so a holder of sign-document in the context could have the update key sign a forged log entry (a proof by did:key: is exactly a log entry's) that adds its own key to the DID, and keep that key after its grant is revoked. sign-document now refuses to sign as a did:key whose key is an active update or pre-rotation key of a did:webvh this VTA holds. Two places in `server::run` were missed, so a TSP-only VTA set up that way refused to start with "no services enabled — enable at least one of REST or DIDComm": - The pre-loop guard, and the restart loop's warning, counted only REST and DIDComm. Both now ask `any_transport_enabled`, which counts REST, DIDComm or TSP, each built and enabled. It is now mirrored in both places, before the unbuilt-TSP check reads it. ### Performance - Use jemalloc in every service binary so freed memory returns to the OS ([#2758](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2758)) The service binaries ran on the system allocator. glibc malloc keeps freed pages in its arenas instead of returning them, so a service's RSS ratchets up to its high-water mark and stays there; on a memory graph that is indistinguishable from a leak (the VTC in particular has been climbing). vtc, vta, vta-enclave, vti-witness, room-host and vti-voting-service now set tikv-jemallocator as the global allocator behind a default-on `jemalloc` feature (non-MSVC only), matching the mediator. jemalloc is tuned through the exported `_rjem_malloc_conf` symbol: background_thread:true (purge while idle) and 5s dirty/muzzy decay. The symbol must carry the `_rjem_` prefix tikv-jemalloc-sys builds with; an unprefixed `malloc_conf` is silently ignored. Both Dockerfiles build with --no-default-features, so they append `jemalloc` to FEATURES for every profile. Each crate now carries the deny-not-forbid unsafe_code lint table for the one exported static, and is listed in scripts/check-workspace-lints.py.

## [0.2.1](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vtc-audit-v0.2.0...vtc-audit-v0.2.1) — 2026-11-18 ### Added - **vtc-service**: Store and serve an uploaded community logo ([#2751](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2751)) * feat(vtc-service): store and serve an uploaded community logo A community can now upload its logo, and the VTC serves it from its own origin, so it shows in the console, the member portal, both sign-in pages and the default landing page wherever the VTC is hosted. Before this, the logo was only the profile's `logoUrl`. Those pages are served with `img-src 'self' data:`, so a logo at any other address was never drawn, and a deployment with nowhere on the VTC's own origin to put a file (a hosted VTC, say) had no logo at all: a filesystem website must have its own host, and `admin_ui.members_dir` is a snapshot that stops following the daemon on every upgrade. Served from memory against a small record read, with a fixed `Content-Type`, `nosniff`, `default-src 'none'; sandbox`, an `ETag` and `304`. Bytes that do not match their record are never served. - A `logo` member (`url`, `sha256`, `mediaType`, `width`, `height`) on the public profile and on `/v1/member/me`'s `community`. Every page draws it in preference to `logoUrl`, which is unchanged. - Console: a Logo card on the Community profile page. title: fix(scripts): resolve repo paths with fileURLToPath so the checks run on Windows
body:
## What and why

`scripts/validate-ceremonies.mjs` and `scripts/lib/schema-bounds.mjs --baseline` derive the repo root from `new URL(..., import.meta.url).pathname`. On Windows that is `/C:/Users/...`, which node's path functions read as relative to the drive root:

- `validate-ceremonies` stops at `no ceremonies/ceremony.meta.schema.json`;
- `schema-bounds --baseline` fails reading `C:\C:\...\specs`.

Both now use `fileURLToPath`, as `build-registry`, `build-go-bindings` and `build-dart-bindings` already do. Nothing changes on Linux or macOS.

Checked on Windows 11, node 22: `validate-ceremonies` validates the three ceremonies; `schema-bounds --baseline` writes the baseline. Before the change, both fail as above.

## Checklist

- [x] Every commit is DCO signed (`git commit -s`).
- [x] The title is a conventional commit; any `!` is scoped to the package whose API breaks.
- [x] If `specs/` changed: all four libraries are regenerated (`npm run regen`) and committed. (No spec changed.)
- [x] No package version and no `CHANGELOG.md` entry is edited — the Release PR does both.
- [x] `npm run check` passes, and the tests for the code touched were run. (On Windows 11, node 22, `npm run check` now completes, including `validate-ceremonies` and `test-ceremonies` (21/21 invalid definitions rejected), which stopped at the first ceremony before.)
